title: Lark and the Glittering Surprise
markdown:
In a realm where the sky kissed jagged peaks and water carved gorges, lived a witch named Lark. Lark was not the sort of witch who conjured storms with a flick of her wrist or brewed potions that turned kings into toads. Her magic was of a subtler, more wonderfully practical sort. She could mend a ripped saddle with a sigh, coax the ripest apple from the gnarliest branch with a hum, and charm a lost lamb back to its mother with a twinkle in her eye. Her home, a cozy cottage nestled amongst the high mountain orchards, was always filled with the scent of drying herbs and the gentle thrum of her quiet enchantments. The walls were adorned with bundles of lavender that released their calming aroma, and shelves overflowed with jars of shimmering dewdrop preserves and sun-kissed berry jams. Outside, her garden was a riot of colour and scent, with moon-petal flowers that unfurled their silver petals only at night and mischievous sprite-berries that giggled when you picked them.

And by her side, always, was Tansy. A stoat with a very sharp mind and unshakeable devotion. His fur, the colour of rich soil after a spring rain, gleamed with health, and his eyes, like polished jet, missed nothing. He was Lark’s shadow, her confidant, and often the quiet force that nudged her towards brilliance. A delicate twitch of his nose had first alerted Lark to a particularly intriguing glint of misplaced moonlight that had accidentally fallen into her tea. A confident chitter had guided her to a patch of forget-me-nots that bloomed even in the deepest snow, tiny blue faces turned skyward. Their bond was not command and obedience, but shared understanding: a silent conversation in the rustle of leaves, the warmth of a shared hearth, and the knowing flick of Tansy’s tail.

In these parts another dabbled in mountain arts: Old Man Hemlock. Not unkind, but pride as strong as the crumbling watchtowers on the highest ridges. He grew enormous pumpkins, plump and polished like regal orbs, and brewed a tea that cured the sniffle in one invigorating sip. Lark and Hemlock shared a polite rivalry: boastful gardening tips, subtly superior spellcasting. She enchanted apples to glow with inner light at dusk; he boasted cabbages the size of boulders, leaves hearty enough to shelter a small family. Good-natured, mostly.

One crisp morning, dawn spilling over snow peaks like molten gold, a peculiar summons arrived. Not a raven. A small intricately carved wooden bird on the doorstep, as if left by a mischievous sprite. Lark wound a tiny almost invisible key. It chirped like tiny bells: “A challenge for the Orchard Queen! The Annual Mountain Blossom Festival approaches, and the prize for the most dazzling display of enchanted fruit shall be eternal bragging rights!”

Lark blinked, a smile unfurling. Eternal bragging rights. Precisely the grand, utterly silly proclamation that sparked mischief in her eye. “Well, Tansy. It seems Old Man Hemlock will be attempting to out-bloom us with his gargantuan gourds.”

Tansy chirped softly, keen gaze on something shimmering near the path. He nudged her hand.

Scattered in dew-kissed grass: tiny discarded scraps of silver foil, a shiny button escaped from a coat, a particularly iridescent beetle wing catching morning light like a fallen jewel.

“Ah. We have company already.”

A peculiar flock haunted these mountains: snow-crows. Not common scavengers pecking crusts. Creatures of aesthetic delight, drawn with almost irresistible compulsion to anything that sparkled, gleamed, or made a delightfully shiny mistake. Notorious for following those who dropped or created such curiosities, hoping to add to their collection of luminous detritus. The more eccentric the sparkle, the more delighted.

Thus Lark and Tansy into the high country, toward the heart of the mountain orchards, air thinning, silence broken by wind in ancient pines and distant goat-bells. Worn satchel of herbs and charms; Tansy trotting, senses alert. The famed Ruined Watchtower: traditional site for the festival’s grandest displays, steeped in forgotten history.

Path through gorges where waterfalls tumbled like liquid silver, roar a constant symphony, air thick with sweet heady apple-bloom. Lark mended a loose stone with a whispered word; coaxed a shy mountain flower a little brighter.

A flutter of wings, black and silver against azure. A flock of snow-crows, then another, soft melodious caws like tiny silver bells. Bright intelligent eyes scanning for misplaced shimmer. A loose buckle on Lark’s boot, a dropped berry gleaming like a ruby, a stray sparkle from a hastily cast charm — all met with delighted attention. They swooped with surprising agility, snatching gently, then continued to follow, numbers growing with each gleam, a shimmering escort.

“Honestly,” Lark chuckled, swatting a bold crow after a loose embroidered thread, “magpies with a penchant for glitter and remarkably poor judgement. One might think they’ve never seen sparkle before.”

Tansy growled low, not anger, mild annoyance. Numerous now, flitting and cawing a distraction from the path. He preferred the mountain’s quiet hum. He noticed, though, their movements seemed less random than Lark suspected: purpose, as if collecting treasures.

Nearing the Ruined Watchtower, solitary sentinel over the valley, weathered stones whispering ancient sentinels, they saw Old Man Hemlock already there. Meticulously arranging prodigious pumpkins polished to mirror sheen reflecting sky, prize-winning cabbages radiating faint earthy glow. He’d even enchanted a cluster of daisies to hum a cheerful slightly off-key tune.

“Ah, Lark!” Voice echoing against ancient stone, robust pride. “Come to witness true horticultural splendor? My pumpkins are already singing your praises, and they aren’t even the main event!”

A polite nod. “Impressive, Hemlock. Truly a sight. Though my enchanted moon-petals are said to glow with a thousand captured fireflies, and my dewdrop preserves to taste of pure starlight.”

Gentle jousting, a familiar ritual, interrupted by a flurry of wings. The snow-crows, now a significant congregation, a blizzard of black and silver, had followed all the way, collection of shiny mistakes adding to their glittering entourage. They perched on crumbling battlements, on Hemlock’s gleaming pumpkins, even — to Lark’s mild consternation — on her shoulders and head, tiny claws surprisingly gentle.

Then the central complication. Hemlock, boundless pride, eternal bragging rights, had a secret weapon: a grand gleaming enchanted watering can of polished copper, imbued with his most potent growth magic, designed to make prize crops burst with even more luminous glory. As he held it aloft to bestow the ultimate blessing, a particularly large exceptionally shiny drop of dew, disturbed by fluttering snow-crows, fell from a nearby apple blossom and landed squarely on the spout. The can, already humming with Hemlock’s magic, overloaded with unintended sparkle, began to vibrate ominously. Not just glowing. Humming, deep, resonant, shaking the watchtower’s foundations, intensity growing.

The snow-crows, tiny bird-brains overwhelmed by this magnificent self-generated sparkle, descended in a glittering vortex, caws a joyful cacophonous chorus. They pecked, flapped, made a glorious shiny mess of Hemlock’s prize display. Pumpkins rolled down the gentle slope. Cabbages tumbled from piles. The humming can threatened to overflow with a cascade of enchanted sparkling dew like a thousand tiny rainbows.

Hemlock threw up his hands, horrified disbelief. “My prize! My eternal bragging rights! Catastrophe!”

Lark watched, quiet contemplation. Not his defeat: the unintended consequence of ambition, amplified by simple gleeful appreciation for shininess. The crows weren’t malicious. Drawn to the most dazzling displays, mistaking intent for inherent brilliance.

Tansy nudged her hand. Keen senses past surface spectacle. Nose toward a small mossy crevice in the watchtower wall, almost hidden. Peeking out: a nest, carefully lined with soft moss, interwoven with tiny precious stones that gleamed with subdued inner light, captured moonlight. Snow-crow fledglings, tiny beaks opening in hopeful anticipation. Understanding washed over Lark. Not collecting shiny mistakes for amusement only. Gathering them, perhaps, to bring back to their young, to adorn nests, to provide little gleams of beauty in a rugged landscape.

She did not shout or unleash flashy spells. From her satchel, a small smooth obsidian stone. Not overtly flashy like Hemlock’s can, but a deep captivating lustre: captured midnight, a fragment of starry sky. She whispered a soft charm, not to create sparkle but to enhance natural allure, an irresistibly inviting beacon of quiet beauty.

“This way, my feathered friends.” Soft, on the breeze, holding out the stone. She walked not away from the watchtower but around it, toward a sheltered sun-drenched ledge overlooking a small crystal-clear mountain pool, surface a mirror of endless sky.

The snow-crows, momentarily distracted from Hemlock’s cascade, darted between falling dew and the intriguing offering. Lark’s stone pulsed with deep alluring gleam. One by one, curiosity and instinct for beauty overriding frenzy, they followed. Tansy, knowing flick of tail, nudged stragglers.

She placed the stone near the pool. A wave of crows followed, earlier frenzy subsiding. They perched at the water’s edge, beaks dipping into cool pure water. Shimmering dew from Hemlock’s can trickled down the watchtower wall in a glittering stream, catching sunlight, but no longer held the singular allure of Lark’s offering or the promise of a communal gathering. Sated with their own kind of sparkle, refreshed, drawn to harmonious gleam and shared experience, they settled. They left Hemlock’s disheveled display, mission of shiny-mistake collection momentarily fulfilled, perhaps to return to young with newfound treasures.

Hemlock, sputtering, brushing stray leaves from his tunic, surveyed the scene. Pumpkins askew, cabbages scattered, but the imminent disaster of the over-enthusiastic watering can averted. The snow-crows, erstwhile tormentors, calmly preening by the pool: far less chaotic, much more picturesque.

Lark approached, mountain blossoms on her cloak. “A bit of an overwhelming display, Hemlock. Sometimes too much shine, too much frantic glitter, can be overwhelming even for the birds. They prefer a gentle gleam to share, perhaps.”

His booming voice a little sheepish, amusement in his eyes. “I suppose I got a little carried away with the eternal bragging rights. It’s been a while since anyone’s challenged me so directly.” A genuine smile, free from usual rivalry, crinkling his eyes. “Clever, Lark. Very clever. You didn’t fight them. You understood them. You saw what they truly needed.”

The Mountain Blossom Festival did not conclude with grand pronouncements of victory or a singular winner. It ended with a shared chuckle as they knelt together, righting pumpkins, gathering cabbages. Lark’s moon-petals still glowed, a soft steady beacon against deepening twilight. Hemlock’s cabbages, though slightly disheveled, still radiated comforting earthiness. The snow-crows, having found a more harmonious way to admire brilliance, flew off, wings leaving a faint ephemeral shimmer on the cooling breeze.

Lark and Tansy returned to their cottage, the scent of mountain blossoms and quiet victory filling the air, a comforting balm. Tansy purred contentedly at her feet, his tail giving a happy little thump against the worn rug. The wooden bird on the doorstep had run down and said nothing more about bragging rights. The obsidian stone stayed by the pool, in case anyone small needed a gleam that did not hum like a disaster. Hemlock, on the walk down, admitted his daisies were still slightly off-key, which Lark considered the most honest horticulture of the day. The festival lanterns, when they were lit along the orchard rows, did not have to compete with a watering can. That, too, was a kind of prize, and Tansy, who had done most of the nudging, claimed it quietly without making a speech.
characters: Lark (witch), Tansy (stoat), Old Man Hemlock (mountain gardener)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
